Pew
PYOO
n. (an inclosed seat in a church)
Webster (1828): [Latin podium.]

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pew as “An inclosed seat in a church.” He notes that “Pews were formerly made square; in modern churches in America they are generally long and narrow, and sometimes called slips.” Rented and owned pews once sorted congregations by wealth. James forbids it: “if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel ... and ye ... say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there” (Jas 2:2–3). His verdict: “Are ye not then partial in yourselves” (Jas 2:4). Jesus told guests to take “the lowest room” (Luk 14:10).

Key Scripture

Jas 2:2 — "For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;"

Jas 2:3 — "And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool:"

Jas 2:4 — "Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?"

Luk 14:10 — "But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee."

1Co 12:27 — "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular."

Modern Corruption

Pew now means any church bench, and is used of a passive audience, the pew against the pulpit; the history of seats sorted by rank is forgotten.

expand to see more

Webster’s pew is “inclosed”: a family’s private seat. Such seats were often rented, and the best ones went to the rich.

James condemned the good place for the gold ring (Jas 2:2–4). The modern habit of calling the congregation the pew, as an audience, has its own danger: every member is a working part of the body (1Co 12:27).
